newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms start offering workers stock options.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms start offering workers stock options.

text.p: A string of Japanese firms have said they will offer stock options to employees since rules on such schemes changed this month, seeing them as likely to boost their share price.
But though the trend is likely to continue for a while, such schemes face a number of hurdles, analysts say.
Stock options could mean firms having to be more responsive to the rights of shareholders -- a novel concept in Japan.
Whether firms adopt stock option schemes "helps us gauge how highly management thinks of investors," said Keiko Kondo, a strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.

"Due to coming deregulation and severe restructuring, companies who are able to buy back shares will become winners and companies who don't have the financial strength to buy them back will lose," she said.

Since the government revised a law that restricted stock options in mid-May, nearly 30 firms, ranging from giant carmaker Toyota Motor Corp to coffee supplier Daiohs Corp, have unveiled plans to offer stock options to their employees.

Some big firms, such as Toyota, have seized on the opportunity to reward shareholders and boost their share price at the same time. The automaker said it would buy back up to 600,000 of its shares worth up to 2.3 billion yen in order to introduce a stock option scheme.

Other firms, such as brokerage Daiwa Securities and game software maker Namco Ltd, have announced plans for such schemes one after another ahead of shareholders' meetings on June 27, when they are expected to be approved.
Analysts said stock options, which confer the right to buy company shares at a specified price after a certain period, would make managers more responsive to shareholders' rights.

Stock options are popular in the U.S. and Europe, where offering a stake in the firm is seen as a way to motivate workers. But analysts also said that while a growing number of Japanese firms are announcing plans to offer stock options, many are holding back until details become clearer.
Electronics giant Sony Corp said it would hold off until the tax treatment of the schemes became clearer.

"It is risky to pin too many hopes on these schemes," said Shinichi Ichikawa, a strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities, although he said stock options would prompt managers to be more sensitive to the rights of investors.
"It's inevitable that companies will actually improve profitability and return on equity (ROE) to let their share prices be reflected in the scheme," he said.

He said stock options could also cause problems, such as widening the gap in salaries between executives and lower-ranked employees and allowing companies to think only of short-term profit and to "window dress" their earnings reports.
Until recently, only venture capital firms in Japan were allowed to offer stock options, mainly because the government needed to make such firms attractive and help them grow.
In late May, parliament passed a revision to the Commercial Code, allowing firms to buy back up to 10 percent of their own shares to be used for stock option schemes.

The measure, which took effect on June 1, is part of the government's five-year "Big Bang" plan to liberalise Japan's financial markets and catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America.
